questionText: For each finding, specify whether it is more consistent with hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia.
rationale: Hypoglycaemia triggers an adrenergic response: tremor, sweating and cool, clammy skin. Hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis (polyuria) and thirst (polydipsia). Fruity breath reflects ketones in diabetic ketoacidosis.
references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes

questionText: For each medication, specify its reversal agent (antidote).
rationale: Protamine neutralises heparin. Vitamin K restores warfarin-inhibited clotting factors. Naloxone reverses opioids, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to prevent liver injury after acetaminophen overdose.
references: Common antidotes — standard pharmacology nursing content

questionText: For each arterial blood gas result, specify the primary acid–base imbalance.
instructions: Reference ranges: pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L.

matrixRows.text: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 56 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L
pH 7.51, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L
pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L
pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 42 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 34 mEq/L

rationale: When the pH is low and the PaCO₂ high, the problem is respiratory acidosis. A high pH with a low PaCO₂ is respiratory alkalosis. A low pH with a low HCO₃⁻ is metabolic acidosis. A high pH with a high HCO₃⁻ is metabolic alkalosis. In each case the other value is normal, so the imbalance is uncompensated.
references: Arterial blood gas interpretation — standard medical-surgical nursing content

scenario: A client is 1 day after a transurethral resection of the prostate and has continuous bladder irrigation through a three-way catheter.
questionText: For each finding, specify whether it is expected or unexpected.

matrixRows.text: Bright red drainage with large clots
Output 300 mL less than the volume of irrigant instilled over 2 hours, with lower abdominal pain
Catheter taped to the thigh with gentle traction

rationale: Light pink drainage, bladder spasms and catheter traction to compress the prostatic fossa are expected after this surgery. Bright red drainage with clots suggests arterial bleeding. Output much lower than the irrigant instilled, with pain, suggests catheter obstruction and bladder distension.
references: Care after TURP — standard medical-surgical nursing content

questionText: At a mass-casualty incident, the nurse uses START triage. For each adult victim, specify the triage category.

matrixRows.text: Walking, with a laceration on the forearm
Not breathing after the airway is repositioned
Not walking; respiratory rate 22/min; no radial pulse
Not walking; respiratory rate 20/min; radial pulse present; follows commands

rationale: In START triage, anyone able to walk is minor. A victim who does not breathe after airway repositioning is deceased or expectant. A respiratory rate above 30/min, absent radial pulse or delayed capillary refill, or inability to follow commands is immediate. Otherwise the victim is delayed.
references: START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) algorithm

questionText: For each insulin, specify its classification.
rationale: Lispro starts working in about 15 minutes and is given with meals. Regular insulin starts in about 30–60 minutes and is the only one listed that is given IV. NPH starts in 1–2 hours and peaks at 4–12 hours. Glargine provides basal coverage for about 24 hours without a pronounced peak.
references: Insulin pharmacokinetics — standard pharmacology nursing content

scenario: The nurse is reviewing the fetal heart rate tracing of a client in active labour at term.
questionText: For each finding, specify whether it is reassuring or non-reassuring.
rationale: A baseline of 110–160/min, moderate variability and early decelerations (caused by head compression) are reassuring. Recurrent late decelerations, absent variability and sustained fetal tachycardia above 160/min are concerning and need intervention.
references: NICHD three-tier fetal heart rate interpretation system

questionText: For each client statement, specify the defence mechanism being used.

matrixRows.text: A client with a new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes says, "The lab must have mixed up my blood."
A client who dislikes a co-worker says, "She is the one who hates me."
After being criticised by a supervisor, a client goes home and yells at their partner.
A student who failed an exam says, "The questions were unfair anyway."

rationale: Denial is refusing to accept reality. Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else. Displacement redirects emotion to a safer target. Rationalisation offers an acceptable-sounding excuse for a failure or behaviour.
references: Defence mechanisms — standard mental health nursing content

questionText: For each wound description, specify the pressure injury stage.

matrixRows.text: Intact skin with an area of non-blanchable redness over the sacrum
Shallow open wound with a pink, moist wound bed and no slough
Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat; no bone or tendon visible
Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone

rationale: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with a viable pink wound bed. Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss in which fat may be visible. Stage 4 is full-thickness loss with exposed bone, tendon, muscle or cartilage.
references: National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) staging definitions (2016)

scenario: A client with a head injury is at risk of increased intracranial pressure.
questionText: For each nursing action, specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

matrixRows.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30°
Keep the head and neck in a neutral, midline position
Group all care activities together into one long session
Suction the airway for 30 seconds at a time
Avoid sharp flexion of the hips

rationale:
Head elevation and a midline neck promote venous drainage from the brain. Stool softeners prevent straining (Valsalva). Avoiding hip flexion limits rises in intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure.

Bundling many activities together raises intracranial pressure, so care is spaced with rest periods. Suctioning is limited to about 10 seconds per pass, with pre-oxygenation.
references: Increased intracranial pressure — standard neurological nursing content

questionText: For each type of viral hepatitis, specify the main route of transmission and whether a vaccine is available in the United States.
instructions: Select all that apply in each row.
rationale: Hepatitis A and E spread by the fecal–oral route, through contaminated food or water. Hepatitis B and C are bloodborne; hepatitis B is also spread sexually and from mother to infant. Vaccines exist for hepatitis A and B. There is no hepatitis C vaccine, and no hepatitis E vaccine is licensed in the United States.
references: CDC: Viral Hepatitis — overview of types A–E

questionText: For each finding, specify the electrolyte imbalance or imbalances with which it is associated.
instructions: Each finding may have more than one answer.

matrixRows.text: Carpal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated (Trousseau's sign)

rationale: U waves are typical of hypokalaemia, and peaked T waves of hyperkalaemia. Trousseau's sign reflects neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia predisposes to kidney stones. Both hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia prolong the QT (or QU) interval, while hypercalcaemia shortens it.
references: Electrolyte imbalances — standard medical-surgical nursing content

questionText: For each antibiotic, specify the adverse effect or effects the nurse should monitor for or teach about.
instructions: Each antibiotic may have more than one answer.
rationale: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, and vancomycin, can damage the kidneys and the eighth cranial nerve, so drug levels, renal function and hearing are monitored. Tetracyclines such as doxycycline and fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin cause photosensitivity; clients use sun protection.
references: Antimicrobial adverse effects — standard pharmacology nursing content

questionText: For each deficit, specify whether it is typically associated with a stroke in the left (dominant) hemisphere, the right hemisphere, or either.
instructions: Each deficit may have more than one answer.

matrixRows.text: Impulsive behaviour and poor safety judgement
Neglect of the left side of the body

rationale: Left-hemisphere strokes usually affect language and cause right-sided weakness, with slow, cautious behaviour. Right-hemisphere strokes cause left-sided neglect, impulsivity and poor judgement. Dysphagia can follow a stroke on either side.
references: Stroke clinical manifestations — standard neurological nursing content

questionText: For each client, specify the personal protective equipment required on entering the room under transmission-based precautions.
instructions: Each client may need more than one item.
rationale: Varicella requires airborne plus contact precautions. Influenza requires droplet precautions (a surgical mask). Tuberculosis requires airborne precautions with a fit-tested N95. C. difficile requires contact precautions (gown and gloves). Standard-precaution gloves are added for any contact with body fluids.
references: CDC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions, Appendix A

questionText: For each finding, specify whether it is associated with hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism or both.
instructions: Each finding may have more than one answer.
rationale: Excess thyroid hormone speeds metabolism: tachycardia and weight loss with a good appetite. Deficiency slows it: cold intolerance and constipation. Fatigue and menstrual changes occur with both.
references: Thyroid disorders — standard medical-surgical nursing content
